doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: New Orleans as a melting pot and Congo Square
summary: Interview with Michael Woods begins; Brunious describes New Orleans' isolation and mixed influences and Congo Square.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: We are filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. And we have with us today a trumpet virtuoso from New Orleans, Wendell Brunious.
Great. Give us some of the color of New Orleans. How and why is New Orleans such a special city for this music?

Well, that’s a big question. That’s really a big question. New Orleans is pretty much a melting pot. I mean the whole, the people of New Orleans, you know the Creole people along with the African people along with the real French people and the South American people and Asians that came there, I mean it. New Orleans is basically an island. So when you came there, you were pretty stuck there, you know what I mean? So I mean not much penetrated New Orleans and it allowed what was there to like generate into what it is, which a lot of people respect and some people don’t. But the music that came out of New Orleans was music from all of those influences, the work song, and then the Latin beat and the French military music, and all of that stuff came to be New Orleans music. And a friend of mine said this: most of the jazz you hear today owes something to Congo Square, which I don’t know if you know what Congo Square is.
I know something of it but I want to get your opinion on it. Tell us about Congo Square.

Well I don’t actually know that much about it. But it was kind of like where, kind of slaves and people of color or whatever you want to call them kind of celebrated their rituals and parties or jazz festivals or whatever they wanted to call it in that day you know?
